What is Slippage?

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date.

DETAILED DEFINITION

Slippage compares an actual execution price with a defined expected or reference price. The comparison requires a side, quantity and timestamp. Paying more than the reference on a purchase is adverse; paying less is favorable. A changing quote, limited available quantity or a delay can contribute to a difference, but a price series alone cannot isolate the cause. A limit price constrains eligible fills and may leave the order unfilled. It does not guarantee both execution and a particular outcome. TradeHQ fills supported market orders at a displayed practice input and does not model actual exchange liquidity.

HOW IT WORKS

Slippage is the difference between a stated reference price and an actual execution price. It can be favorable or adverse; volatile conditions, limited liquidity and delays may increase it.

KEY POINTS
Difference between expected and actual execution price
Quote changes, liquidity constraints and delays can affect slippage even outside volatile periods
Limit prices constrain eligible fills but do not ensure execution; market fills can differ from a quote
💡 WHY THIS MATTERS

Compare expected and weighted-average fill prices, with fees stated separately. A limit price can constrain execution but may leave the order unfilled; neither order type removes every risk.

Worked exercise and its limits

For an imagined 100-unit buy, a $10.05 fill versus an expected $10 costs $5 more. A $9.98 fill saves $2. Define the reference quote and timestamp; slippage can be favorable or adverse and differs from a separately charged commission.

References and scope
SEC Investor.gov — market, limit and stop order mechanics
